title: Osteoporosis: Treat Fracture Risk, Not the T-Score Alone
bottomLine: Osteoporosis treatment decisions are fracture-risk decisions. Use fragility-fracture history, Canadian FRAX/CAROC risk, BMD and age/clinical risk together; when pharmacotherapy is indicated, bisphosphonates are first-line for many patients, while denosumab or anabolic therapy has specific indications and discontinuation/transition requirements.
recognize: Prior hip/vertebral or multiple fragility fractures and recent fractures strongly increase near-term fracture risk.
A T-score alone does not capture falls, prior fracture, glucocorticoids, parental hip fracture, frailty or other risk drivers.
differentiate: Osteopenia with high FRAX risk can warrant treatment, while a low BMD result still requires evaluation for secondary causes and treatment suitability.
Osteomalacia/mineralization disorders are different from primary osteoporosis and should not be treated as BMD-only osteoporosis.
assessment: Assess fragility fractures, falls, height loss, glucocorticoids, smoking/alcohol, menopause/hypogonadism, renal disease, malabsorption and medication contributors.
Assess dental/esophageal/renal factors and ability to adhere to the chosen therapy.
workup: Use BMD and Canada-specific FRAX (preferred) or CAROC when indicated, plus calcium, phosphate, creatinine, ALP, TSH and cause-directed secondary workup.
Use vertebral imaging when clinical/FRAX/BMD features make occult spine fracture plausible.
management: Use exercise/falls prevention, adequate nutrition/calcium/vitamin D and pharmacotherapy according to fracture risk.
Bisphosphonates are first-line for many initiating therapy; denosumab is an option for selected contraindication/intolerance/access contexts and requires a long-term/transition plan.
Seek osteoporosis expertise for very high-risk/recent severe vertebral fracture or anabolic-therapy consideration.
medicationSafety: Denosumab doses should not be casually delayed/stopped because rapid bone loss and vertebral fractures can follow; plan antiresorptive transition when stopping.
Bisphosphonate renal/GI/dental and rare atypical-fracture/ONJ risks require context, not blanket avoidance.
counselling: Explain that fracture prevention—not chasing a BMD number—is the treatment goal and that some drugs require planned transition rather than abrupt stopping.
followUp: Reassess fracture risk/adherence and BMD at guideline-supported intervals, sooner for new fracture or major new risk.
examTrap: Starting or stopping osteoporosis drugs solely from the T-score without calculating fracture risk or planning denosumab transition.
oneLinePearl: Osteoporosis treatment follows fracture risk; denosumab needs an exit plan before it starts.

title: Metabolic Bone Disease: Calcium, Phosphate, PTH, Vitamin D, Kidney, and Bone Turnover Tell the Story
bottomLine: Metabolic bone disease is broader than osteoporosis. When fractures, bone pain, abnormal calcium/phosphate/ALP, renal disease or unexpectedly low BMD suggest a mineralization or secondary process, interpret calcium, phosphate, PTH, vitamin D, kidney function and alkaline phosphatase together before applying an osteoporosis drug algorithm.
recognize: Osteomalacia can present with bone pain, muscle weakness and fractures with vitamin-D/phosphate abnormalities.
CKD-mineral bone disorder, hyperparathyroidism, malabsorption and medication effects can produce abnormal bone density and fracture risk through different mechanisms.
differentiate: Osteoporosis is reduced bone strength with normally mineralized bone; osteomalacia is impaired mineralization.
A high ALP may be bone or liver in origin and requires context.
assessment: Assess fracture type, bone pain, muscle weakness, renal disease, GI/malabsorption, bariatric history, diet, medications and endocrine disease.
Look for renal stones, deformity and signs of calcium/phosphate disorders.
workup: Use calcium, phosphate, ALP, creatinine/eGFR, PTH and vitamin D plus cause-directed tests; use BMD/imaging where it answers fracture/structure questions.
Do not interpret one abnormal calcium/PTH value without repeat/physiologic context.
management: Treat the underlying mineral/endocrine/renal cause before or alongside fracture-prevention therapy.
Refer complex CKD-MBD, unexplained hypophosphatemia, severe secondary hyperparathyroidism or suspected rare metabolic bone disease.
medicationSafety: Antiresorptives can worsen hypocalcemia if calcium/vitamin-D physiology is not corrected first.
Renal function materially affects some osteoporosis therapies and phosphate/vitamin-D treatment.
counselling: Explain why 'weak bones' can result from different mineral/hormone problems and therefore need different treatment.
followUp: Trend the biochemical abnormality that defines the disease plus fracture/bone outcomes.
examTrap: Giving a bisphosphonate for low BMD caused by untreated osteomalacia without correcting the mineralization defect.
oneLinePearl: Low BMD tells you bone is weak; mineral labs tell you why.

title: Pituitary Adenoma: Ask Two Questions—Is It Secreting, and Is It Compressing?
bottomLine: Pituitary adenoma evaluation has two parallel tasks: identify hormone excess/deficiency and identify mass effect. Visual-field symptoms, acute severe headache/ophthalmoplegia or adrenal insufficiency can make a pituitary lesion urgent; hormone testing must be syndrome-directed rather than a random panel.
recognize: Prolactinoma can cause amenorrhea/galactorrhea/hypogonadism; GH excess causes acromegaly; ACTH excess causes Cushing disease.
Mass effect can cause bitemporal visual loss, headache or cranial-nerve deficits; nonfunctioning macroadenoma can cause hypopituitarism.
differentiate: Mild prolactin elevation can result from medication, pregnancy, hypothyroidism or stalk effect and is not automatically a prolactinoma.
Pituitary apoplexy is an emergency distinct from routine incidental adenoma.
assessment: Assess visual symptoms, headache, menstrual/sexual/reproductive function, galactorrhea, growth/acromegaly/Cushing features and symptoms of adrenal/thyroid deficiency.
Review antipsychotic/antiemetic and other prolactin-elevating medications.
workup: Use targeted prolactin, IGF-1, cortisol-axis, thyroid-axis and gonadal testing according to lesion/symptoms.
Use pituitary MRI and formal visual fields when lesion size/location warrants them.
management: Treat prolactinoma primarily with dopamine agonist in appropriate cases; other functioning/nonfunctioning macroadenomas often require endocrinology/neurosurgical care.
Replace deficient hormones in safe order, addressing adrenal insufficiency before thyroid hormone when both are possible.
medicationSafety: Dopamine agonists require orthostasis/psychiatric/impulse effects review.
Do not start levothyroxine in untreated central adrenal insufficiency without adrenal protection.
counselling: Explain that pituitary lesions can affect both hormone production and nearby vision/brain structures.
followUp: Coordinate hormone, imaging and visual-field surveillance according to lesion type/response.
examTrap: Calling mild medication-related prolactin elevation a prolactinoma or treating central hypothyroidism before checking the adrenal axis.
oneLinePearl: Pituitary mass: is it secreting, is it compressing, and what hormone functions has it suppressed?
sourceBasis: BC Hormone Testing — Indications and Appropriate Use

title: PCOS: Treat Reproductive Symptoms and Long-Term Metabolic Risk Together
bottomLine: PCOS is a reproductive-metabolic syndrome. Establish the diagnosis only after excluding important mimics, then manage menstrual/endometrial protection, hyperandrogenic symptoms, fertility goals and cardiometabolic risk without assuming every patient has obesity or insulin resistance.
recognize: Irregular/absent ovulation, clinical/biochemical hyperandrogenism and polycystic ovarian morphology can contribute to diagnostic criteria depending on age/context.
PCOS is associated with diabetes risk, dyslipidemia, OSA, mental-health burden and endometrial risk from prolonged anovulation.
differentiate: Pregnancy, thyroid disease, hyperprolactinemia, nonclassic CAH and androgen-secreting/Cushing disorders can mimic PCOS.
Adolescent irregular cycles require age-post-menarche context; ultrasound should not be used casually to label normal pubertal ovarian morphology PCOS.
assessment: Assess menstrual pattern, hyperandrogenism, pregnancy/fertility goals, eating/weight stigma, BP, diabetes risk, sleep apnea, mood and medications.
Look for rapid virilization or severe androgen elevation suggesting another cause.
workup: Exclude pregnancy and key endocrine mimics; assess glucose and cardiovascular risk according to patient risk/PCOS context.
Use androgen/other testing when results will refine diagnosis or exclude dangerous mimics.
management: Use health-behaviour support without weight stigma and treat metabolic risk factors directly.
Provide endometrial protection through regular progestin exposure/combined hormonal therapy when appropriate, and treat hirsutism/acne/fertility based on goals.
Metformin can be useful for metabolic/glycemic indications and selected reproductive contexts but is not a universal treatment for every PCOS symptom.
medicationSafety: Combined hormonal contraception requires VTE/contraindication review; antiandrogens require reliable contraception because of fetal risk.
Do not use weight-loss medication in pregnancy and coordinate conception plans.
counselling: Explain that PCOS is not caused by lack of willpower and that goals can focus on cycles, fertility, skin/hair symptoms, metabolic health or all of these.
followUp: Track cycles/endometrial protection, metabolic risk, mental health and treatment goals over time.
examTrap: Diagnosing PCOS from ovarian ultrasound alone or treating all PCOS with metformin regardless of the patient's actual goals and metabolic status.
oneLinePearl: PCOS care has two timelines: today's reproductive symptoms and tomorrow's metabolic risk.

title: Lipid Disorders: Diagnose the Pattern, Estimate Risk, Then Treat the Vascular Problem
bottomLine: Dyslipidemia management is risk-based. Identify secondary causes and severe inherited patterns, calculate Canadian cardiovascular risk when applicable, recognize statin-indicated/high-risk conditions and distinguish LDL-focused vascular prevention from severe hypertriglyceridemia where pancreatitis risk changes the immediate priority.
recognize: Clinical ASCVD, most diabetes/CKD contexts and LDL-C ≥5 mmol/L are important statin-indicated/high-risk groups in CCS guidance.
Very high triglycerides require evaluation for secondary causes and pancreatitis risk.
differentiate: Primary prevention uses absolute-risk context; secondary prevention after ASCVD uses more intensive lipid lowering.
Familial hypercholesterolemia should be considered with severe LDL elevation/premature ASCVD/family pattern.
assessment: Assess ASCVD, diabetes, CKD, thyroid disease, alcohol, medications, pregnancy, family history and diet/metabolic contributors.
Review prior statin tolerance and actual adherence/access.
workup: Use fasting or nonfasting lipid testing as appropriate; consider ApoB/non-HDL and one-time Lp(a) according to CCS guidance.
Investigate secondary causes when the pattern is severe or unexpected.
management: Use statin therapy according to vascular risk/statin-indicated conditions and add nonstatin therapy when thresholds/residual risk justify it.
Treat severe hypertriglyceridemia and its secondary causes with pancreatitis prevention in mind.
medicationSafety: Review drug interactions and evaluate true severe muscle/hepatic adverse effects rather than routine CK surveillance.
counselling: Explain absolute cardiovascular benefit and why treatment intensity may be high even when the LDL value does not look dramatic.
followUp: Repeat lipids after treatment changes to confirm response/adherence and reassess risk over time.
examTrap: Treating the highest LDL number in the room more aggressively than established ASCVD—or ignoring severe triglycerides with abdominal pain.
oneLinePearl: Lipids are treated in the context of vascular and pancreatitis risk, not by ranking numbers alone.

title: Obesity Pharmacotherapy: Match the Medication to Complications, Goals, Safety, and Long-Term Use
bottomLine: Obesity is a chronic disease and pharmacotherapy is a long-term treatment option, not a short-term willpower aid. Use adiposity-related complications plus anthropometrics, patient goals, contraindications, interactions, cost/access and treatment preference to select among medications approved in Canada, and anticipate weight/health-benefit regression if effective therapy is stopped.
recognize: Obesity-related complications include diabetes, hypertension, OSA, HFpEF, MASH, osteoarthritis and mechanical/mental-health effects.
BMI alone incompletely describes adiposity burden and should not erase complication severity or patient goals.
differentiate: Obesity pharmacotherapy is not the same as prescribing a diabetes dose/brand of a similar molecule for a nonapproved purpose.
Compounded or unapproved weight-loss medications are not equivalent to Health Canada-approved therapy.
assessment: Ask permission to discuss weight/adiposity; assess complications, eating-disorder symptoms, medications, pregnancy plans, cardiovascular/psychiatric history, GI disease and access/cost.
Set functional/metabolic/quality-of-life goals, not weight alone.
workup: Screen for obesity-related complications and medication contraindications; do not order broad endocrine tests without a clinical suspicion.
Assess pregnancy before starting contraindicated pharmacotherapy when relevant.
management: Offer evidence-based obesity pharmacotherapy with health-behaviour support to eligible adults according to the 2025 Obesity Canada guideline.
Current Canadian options include GLP-1/GIP-based and other approved agents selected to the patient's complications and safety profile.
Continue effective therapy long term when benefits exceed harms and align with goals.
medicationSafety: Avoid weight-management pharmacotherapy in pregnancy/breastfeeding and review class-specific GI, gallbladder/pancreatic, BP/HR, psychiatric, interaction and contraindication issues.
Do not use compounded/unapproved medications as routine obesity treatment.
redFlags: Rapid unexplained weight loss suggesting another disease
counselling: Use non-stigmatizing chronic-disease language and discuss expected long-term treatment, cost/access and what stopping therapy may mean.
followUp: Track health complications, tolerability, function, weight trajectory and patient priorities; change therapy when ineffective/intolerable rather than blaming adherence.
examTrap: Telling a patient to 'try harder' before offering evidence-based pharmacotherapy or using compounded weight-loss medication as if it were equivalent to an approved product.
oneLinePearl: Choose obesity medication for the whole patient and plan for chronic treatment, not a temporary number on the scale.
sourceBasis: Obesity Canada 2025 Pharmacotherapy in Obesity Management Update

title: Sodium and Potassium Disorders: Treat Neurologic and Cardiac Risk While You Find the Cause
bottomLine: Sodium disorders are disorders of water/tonicity and potassium disorders are cardiac/neuromuscular emergencies when severe. Assess symptoms, ECG and tempo first, then determine volume/renal/medication/endocrine causes; correction must be controlled because both undertreatment and overly rapid correction can injure the patient.
recognize: Severe hyponatremia can cause confusion, seizure and cerebral edema; chronic hyponatremia is vulnerable to osmotic demyelination if corrected too rapidly.
Severe hyperkalemia can cause conduction changes/arrhythmia; ECG can be normal despite dangerous potassium and does not replace the laboratory value/clinical context.
differentiate: Hyponatremia should be classified by tonicity and volume/urine physiology rather than sodium alone.
Pseudohyperkalemia from specimen hemolysis/thrombocytosis/leukocytosis must be considered when the patient/ECG do not fit.
assessment: Assess neurologic symptoms, volume status, renal function, GI losses, medications, glucose, adrenal/thyroid clues and fluid intake.
For potassium, obtain ECG and review RAAS drugs, MRA, potassium supplements, diuretics, insulin/acidosis and renal function.
workup: Use serum osmolality, glucose and urine sodium/osmolality when they answer the hyponatremia question.
Repeat suspected pseudohyperkalemia appropriately but do not delay treatment of a convincing dangerous result.
management: Severe symptomatic hyponatremia requires controlled hypertonic-saline protocol and frequent monitoring; chronic/asymptomatic treatment targets cause and safe correction rate.
Dangerous hyperkalemia separates three jobs: stabilize myocardium when indicated, shift potassium intracellularly, and remove potassium from the body.
Treat hypokalemia with route/rate determined by severity, symptoms, ECG and ongoing losses.
medicationSafety: Overrapid sodium correction can cause osmotic demyelination; overrapid potassium replacement can cause fatal arrhythmia.
Stop/review culprit drugs without reflexively abandoning prognostic RAAS therapy when a safe corrective plan is possible.
counselling: Explain medication/fluid/diet contributors in the context of the diagnosed cause rather than generic salt/potassium restriction.
followUp: Trend electrolytes at a frequency proportional to severity and treatment; close the loop on endocrine/renal causes.
examTrap: Correcting chronic hyponatremia rapidly to normalize the lab or treating hyperkalemia with insulin alone without stabilizing/removing potassium when needed.
oneLinePearl: Sodium threatens the brain; potassium threatens the heart—tempo and cause decide the safe correction.

title: Calcium Disorders: Confirm the Calcium, Read PTH Physiology, Treat Symptoms First
bottomLine: Confirm clinically meaningful hyper- or hypocalcemia using corrected or ionized calcium when appropriate, then let PTH tell you whether the physiology is PTH-mediated. Severe symptomatic calcium disorders require immediate stabilization while the endocrine, malignant, renal, medication or vitamin-D cause is worked up.
recognize: Hypercalcemia can cause polyuria, dehydration, constipation, cognitive change and arrhythmia; severe disease can cause AKI/encephalopathy.
Hypocalcemia can cause perioral paresthesia, cramps/tetany, seizure and QT prolongation.
differentiate: High calcium with nonsuppressed PTH suggests PTH-mediated disease; suppressed PTH shifts the differential toward malignancy, vitamin-D/granulomatous and other causes.
Low calcium with high PTH suggests secondary response (vitamin-D deficiency/CKD etc.); low/inappropriate PTH suggests hypoparathyroidism.
assessment: Review symptoms, cancer, stones, fractures, neck surgery, kidney disease, medications (thiazide/lithium/bisphosphonate/denosumab), supplements and vitamin-D exposure.
Assess hydration, neurologic status and ECG when severe.
workup: Confirm calcium and use PTH, phosphate, magnesium, creatinine/eGFR and vitamin-D studies as indicated.
Use PTHrP, SPEP, imaging or other cause-directed testing only when the physiology/differential supports it.
management: Severe symptomatic hypercalcemia needs acute hydration/cause-specific therapy and malignancy/endocrine care as appropriate.
Severe symptomatic hypocalcemia requires monitored IV calcium plus magnesium correction when needed.
Treat chronic disease according to its cause rather than repeatedly correcting the number alone.
medicationSafety: Denosumab/bisphosphonates can worsen hypocalcemia when vitamin-D/calcium physiology is inadequate.
counselling: Explain that calcium disorders are hormone/renal/mineral problems; supplements are not automatically the solution.
followUp: Trend calcium and the disease-defining labs after treatment; ensure malignancy/endocrine/renal referrals are closed-loop.
examTrap: Ordering parathyroid imaging before checking PTH physiology or giving more calcium/vitamin D to every low-calcium result without checking magnesium/renal/PTH context.
oneLinePearl: Confirm the calcium, ask PTH which direction the physiology is pointing, then treat the dangerous symptoms and the cause.
